People have been discussing over the removal over the downvote button as it ultimately serves as a biased tool to silence those who are vocal but against the majority's opinion and thus stops others from speaking out.

Today we can have people stuck at -45 for a comment that really isn't offending but some groups might think it's good for their own agendas or bias. I.e Apple vs Microsoft/Windows vs Linux discussions are a prime example. Some reply chains I noticed are very constructive to the discussion but got hidden because people didn't agree to what was being said and that's a shame.

But it would be rather nice if comments could not go under 0 and instead be treated as a normal comment that sparks discussion even if it is negative.

What do you think, guys?
In regard to downvote removal discussion, can't we just have points capped at min. 0?

I was thinking of a per-subverse parameter, call it "downvoat freeze" so each subverse could specify its own minimum. When a post gets to that point, it should alert the mods because if a post or comment is getting so many downvoats it probably needs some sort of moderator intervention.

That intervention could include - remove the post/comment, remove the downvoat freeze (thus allowing the post to continue sinking no longer limited by the freeze), or do nothing (i.e., allow the post/comment to stay as-is).

Recently I've been trying to wrap my head around how the system really works, and if it actually provides a better quality of care.

From what I can gather, the United States seems to have a greater 5 year survival rate for most cancers than most other countries and even a lower mortality rate if you factor out violent accidents/deaths. Is that a fair assessment?

I know that we pay an absurd amount for healthcare when comparing us to other industrialized nations, but I'm curious if we actually get better healthcare as a result.
Voaters, what do you think of America's healthcare system?

As someone from a country with free healthcare, I think America's system is awful. It neglects those who really need it, or cripples them with debt, and it leaves lots of room for profiteering from people in need.

It does have one thing going for it, though, and that's the amount of money. Lots of research, and over-zealous testing means the quality of care is higher, though often unnecessary.

Here in the UK, there's a lot of waiting with the NHS (National Health Service), but if you really need it, it's almost immediate. Drugs are cheap or free, and everything is available to everyone including tourists (for the most part).

I think the best part of the system here is that there are ample public hospitals that set a very high standard, but there are also private hospitals which then have to compete with the public hospitals in terms of quality and pricing.

I've not had much experience with the civilian side of things, but i can tell you the VA is completely and utterly fucked. 2 years ago i had an MRI done and they found i had a torn and detached labrum in my left hip. They referred me to another VA that had a more dedicated othropedic department that was 150 miles away. They tested for just about everything....numerous xrays, flexibility tests, etc. Now, 2 years later and not only have we not addressed the MRI but the doctor also suggested sciatic as the root cause. Seriously? Not to mention it's nigh on impossible to get an appointment, and when you do you get maybe 15 minutes to discuss issues with the doctor, at which point they throw pills at you and send you on your way.
